newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: On the Internet you better not cry....
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: On the Internet you better not cry....

text.p: Sign of the times: Santa Claus is on the Internet and he appears to be hooked on e-mail.
In fact, jolly old St. Nick is all over the Net, which of course is befitting of his magical powers.
It is clear the dear old man of the North Pole has not had any problems moving to the digital world, while also maintaining his quaint cadre of elves and cumbersome sleigh-based distribution system.
A simple search for "Santa Claus" on the Lycos search engine turned up 34,211 documents out of a search of some 60 million pages.

Surf the Net and you will find Santa has his own "FAQ," for frequently asked questions about the jolly one, his own paranoid X-mas Files based on the popular American television show, X-Files, and numerous ways to communicate with him via e-mail.

A dangerously funny site was a lawsuit purportedly being launched by a group calling itself the ACLU (http://www.cs.nps.navy.mil/people/support/akin/Funny/ACLUvsSant a.html). The suit accuses Santa with violating children's
right to privacy, among other things. It hones in on an alleged Santa-related memo with these lines: "He sees when you're awake/he knows when you've been bad or good/so be good for goodness'sake."

Said ACLU spokesman E. Scrooge: "It is obvious Mr. Claus has violated the children's rights, as we have alleged in our suit, because of the memos and other company information we have obtained. In addition, we believe Mr. Claus has been engaging in mind control experiments designed to prevent the free expression of beliefs."

The easiest-to-remember site has to be the santaclaus.com page (http://www.santaclaus.com), which offers a trove of information on the big guy. It receives some 150,000 "hits" a day plus some 6,000 e-mail messages from Claus fans, according to some well-informed elves from the site.
"I have been a good girl this past year and I have been getting good grades at school," reads a letter from B.B. "This first thing that I'm wishing for is a cure for cancer."
Miami-based Coral Tech Inc registered the santaclaus domain name in 1994 and had the first Santa site running for Christmas of the same year, according to an elf named Sara at Coral.

"We have seen an incredible increase in the number of letters from school children -- entire classes write letters from as varied places as Singapore, the Dominican Republic, Canada and Germany," she said.
For the non believers out there check out: http://www.uni-karlsruhe.de/Gregor.Heinen/Einzelnes/santa.html.

The author of a reprinted article makes a scientifically savage assault on Santa's magical abilities. The author estimated that Santa must visit 91.8 million homes on Christmas Eve and since he has 31 hours to accomplish his task (taking into account all the times zones) he must make 822.6 visits per second.

"This means that Santa's sleigh is moving at 650 miles per second, 3,000 times the speed of sound. In comparison, the fastest man-made vehicle on earth, the Ulysses space probe, moves at a pokey 27.4 miles per second."

It was estimated Santa would really need 214,200 reindeer to pull his sleigh payload of 353,430 tons. This kind of tonnage would face enormous air resistance hurtling around the world and would heat to extreme temperatures, similar to the way spacecraft heat up re-entering the earth's atmosphere.

The author even throws cold water on the multiple Santa theory, which has gained popularity of late with the numerous sightings of the gentleman in the red tunic at the various shopping malls and on street corners.
"It seems likely that a megasanta, while perhaps avoiding vaporized reindeer, would suffer huge casualties from in-air collisions," the article concluded.
More ardent Santa fans, however, would say "humbug" to all this and still find a way to wish a merry holiday season for all.
